summary: US-023 (SPLIT into TKT-179..182): orphan-seat prevention, per map
description:
**As** an organizer, **I want** the system to stop buyers leaving single unsellable seats between parties, **so that** I do not finish the on-sale with a row full of gaps I can never sell.

**Priority:** P2  **Depends on:** TKT-174 (a picker to refuse a selection in)

**The third epic COS**, and the only one with no existing machinery: *"Orphan-single-seat prevention rules configurable per map."* An orphan is a free seat with no free neighbour left in its row after a selection is taken. Preventing it is standard practice in reserved seating and is worth real revenue; making it **configurable per map** matters because the rule is wrong for some venues (general-admission-style rows, boxes, accessible pairs).

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] A seat map carries an orphan-prevention setting owned by catalog alongside the geometry, defaulting to **off** so every existing map behaves exactly as it does today.
- [ ] With the rule on, a seat selection whose commitment would leave a free seat with no free neighbour in its row is refused **server-side, at claim time** — the arbiter is the same transaction that decides the claim, not the browser. A refusal names the seat(s) that would be stranded.
- [ ] The rule reads the seat map version the pool is seated against, so an edit that republishes the map cannot silently change the rule applied to a live claim (ADR-029: a published version is immutable).
- [ ] With the rule off, behaviour is byte-identical to TKT-173's: no extra read, no extra latency on the claim path.
- [ ] Row ends are handled explicitly and deliberately: a seat at the end of a row has one neighbour, not two, and the rule must state and test what it does there.
- [ ] The picker surfaces the refusal legibly and the map stays usable afterwards (the buyer can adjust the selection without reloading).
- [ ] The rule is exercised under the seated contention test: concurrent claimants cannot each pass the check and jointly strand a seat — the check is only real if it holds under the transaction that decides.
- [ ] Spec declared, generated code committed before the gate, smoke coverage (ADR-009 / ADR-028 / ADR-030).

Quality gates: `make check` green; contract tests; browser submit evidence for the UI surface. **This ticket moves no money.**

objective.note: It is the epic's third COS and the only one with no existing machinery; without it the epic closes incomplete.

scope.note: IN: the per-map setting, server-side enforcement at claim time, row-end semantics, the UI surface, the contention proof. OUT: adjacency-aware best-available (TKT-81), price-tier or accessibility-seat rules, multi-row party splitting, retro-fitting the rule to already-sold maps.

uncertainties.note: Resolved at Planning under the owner-waived gate protocol (was owner: human). **Where the check runs is a real architectural decision, not a coin flip.** Inventory decides the claim and knows occupancy but holds seat identities as opaque `section/row/seat` strings — it has no row ordering. Catalog owns the geometry and the rule but does not decide claims. Three candidate shapes: (a) inventory calls catalog on the claim path — simplest, but puts a synchronous cross-service call inside the hottest transaction in the system, which ADR-010 exists to keep short; (b) inventory caches the row layout from the `seat_map.published` event it already consumes — no hot-path call, at the cost of a projection to keep correct; (c) the check runs in commerce between the price resolution and the claim — no hot-path cost, but it is then advisory, and a check that does not run inside the deciding transaction cannot satisfy the contention AC. Planning must choose and record a reason; the choice likely warrants an ADR.

dependencies.note: blocked-by TKT-174. Nothing outside this epic is open.

approach.note: Follows from the uncertainty above. Inventory's consumer already receives catalog seat-map events and already holds a catalog HTTP client for pinning, so both (a) and (b) have an existing seam — which one is right is Planning's call.

first_slice.note: A single row of five seats with the rule on: selecting seats 1 and 2 is refused because seat 3 would strand against an already-taken 4; selecting 1-3 succeeds.

success.note: Demoable in the browser: turn the rule on for a map, try to strand a seat, get refused with the seat named.

context_memo.note: Baked at decomposition (2026-08-01). Re-resolve at claim — this is the last ticket of the epic and three others land before it.

binding.rule: Local gate: `make check` (lint + test + build, Go & TS, plus the gateway smoke suite; run `make deps` first on a clean clone). CI runs the same gate — keep them mirrored. Commit regenerated code (`openapi_gen.go`, `api-types.gen.ts`) before running the gate — `check-generate` diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift and fails the run.

reference.summary: Epic lineage and capability map (US-017/US-018 are the seat-claim core; this epic is the buyer-facing picker)

governingAdrs.why: The claim transaction is the hottest path in the platform and is deliberately kept short and lock-ordered. A synchronous cross-service call added inside it is the single most expensive thing this ticket could do — if Planning chooses that shape, it must justify it against this ADR, not around it.

Seat claim/pin coordination: `released_at IS NULL` is liveness, and expired holds are swept lazily. An orphan check that counts a lazily-unswept expired hold as occupying a seat will refuse a legal selection.

A published seat-map version is immutable and an edit mints a NEW version; a pool is seated against one specific version. The rule and the geometry it reads must both come from the version the pool names, or a republish silently changes the rule under a live claim. Also: the family-scoped advisory lock, not a row lock, is what closes the edit-vs-claim race.

If the check reads geometry, it reads the hours tier — legitimately cacheable. If it reads occupancy, that is the seconds tier and inside the deciding transaction it must not be read from any cache at all.
Whatever query backs the rule, a scoped read is only scoped if an index backs the filter — and proving it takes two tests.
Contract-first: the per-map setting is a catalog contract change; generated code committed before the gate.

<!-- sdlc:stage=ready kind=claim -->
### Claimed — TKT-175

**Selection reason.** The epic's last child. Its only blocker, TKT-174, merged as `762ee6fc`. Nothing else in flight.

**Blocker check.** `blocked-by TKT-174` — Done. Zero open blockers.

**Branch.** `TKT-175-orphan-seat-rules`, cut from `origin/main` at `762ee6fc`.

**⚠️ Gate waiver.** Runs **gateless** under the standing owner waiver for TKT-35. Recorded again here: this is the fourth and last child to run without human gates, and the epic therefore closes with **no control arm** — TKT-173's and TKT-174's retros both asked for one and both were overruled by the standing instruction, correctly.

**Model routing** unchanged: plan `gpt-5.6-sol` · planReview `main-agent` · implement `main-agent` · aiReview `gpt-5.6-sol`. Both cross-model pairs differ. ✅

---

### This ticket carries the epic's only genuine architectural decision

The other three children had implementation choices. This one has a boundary problem, and it was recorded at decomposition rather than discovered late:

> Inventory decides the claim and knows occupancy, but holds seat identities as **opaque `section/row/seat` strings** — it has no row ordering. Catalog owns the geometry and the rule but does not decide claims.

An orphan is a free seat with no free neighbour left **in its row** after a selection is taken. Deciding that needs the row's ordered seats *and* live occupancy *and* the deciding transaction — and no single service has all three today.

**One fact checked at claim time that narrows the field:** inventory does **not** consume seat-map events. `services/inventory/internal/consumer/consumer.go` filters exactly four subjects — `performance.published`, `.archived`, `.closed`, `.reopened`. There is no `seat_map.published` subscription and no geometry projection. So the "inventory keeps a cached row layout" option is not a small addition to an existing consumer; it is a new subscription, a new projection, and a new thing that can be stale. The decomposition note called it "no hot-path call, at the cost of a projection to keep correct" — the cost is larger than that phrasing suggests, and Planning should price it honestly.

### Stop-condition pre-check

- **Auth:** untouched.
- **Money:** untouched — this refuses a claim, it prices nothing.
- **Data migrations:** at least one is likely (a per-map setting in catalog). Additive settings on an existing table are anticipated by the ticket's own AC ("a seat map carries an orphan-prevention setting owned by catalog"). Anything beyond that — a new table for a geometry projection in inventory, say — is a consequence of the architectural choice and must be **named in the plan before it is written**, not discovered in the diff.
- **CI/deploy:** none expected.
- **The hot path:** ADR-010's claim transaction is the platform's most contended. If the plan puts a synchronous cross-service call inside it, that is a decision requiring an explicit argument against ADR-010, and it is the one thing on this ticket I will not accept by default.

### Scope reminder

IN: the per-map setting, server-side enforcement at claim time, row-end semantics, the picker's surfacing of the refusal, the contention proof. OUT: adjacency-aware best-available (TKT-81), price-tier or accessibility-seat rules, multi-row party splitting, retro-fitting the rule to already-sold maps.

<!-- sdlc:stage=planning kind=plan -->
### Execution plan — TKT-175 (draft)

**Drafted by `gpt-5.6-sol`** (codex, effort high, read-only), per `config.models.plan`. Job `task-msbdmgiv-w8j5ap`, completed, conclusive.

The brief gave it the eight ACs, the boundary problem stated as the point of the ticket, the four candidate shapes with their costs, the fact (checked at claim time) that inventory consumes no seat-map events, and the seven governing ADRs. It was told explicitly not to pick by elegance, and that AC7 and AC4 are the discriminators.

---

## 1. Definition of Done

- [ ] **AC1:** Catalog persists `orphan_prevention_enabled` on each `seat_maps` version, `NOT NULL DEFAULT false`; create/edit APIs and back-office controls expose it, and existing maps remain off.
- [ ] **AC2:** An enabled seated claim runs the orphan check after lazy expiry and contention arbitration, under the `inventory_pools ... FOR UPDATE` lock, before any claim write; a 409 returns every newly stranded identity.
- [ ] **AC3:** Inventory projects adjacency from the exact `seat_map_id` carried by the pool’s publication. Editing/republishing the family cannot alter a live pool’s rule or topology.
- [ ] **AC4:** Disabled maps retain schema-4 publication bytes and today’s claim responses. They perform no catalog geometry fetch during provisioning and no adjacency query on the claim path.
- [ ] **AC5:** Tests pin immediate ordered-neighbour semantics, both row ends, multi-row isolation, position gaps, and one-seat rows.
- [ ] **AC6:** Storefront displays the stranded identities, preserves the selection, keeps the stranded seats selectable, and lets the buyer adjust without reload.
- [ ] **AC7:** A real-Postgres seated contention test proves two individually legal claims cannot jointly strand a seat; one commits and the serialized loser returns that seat’s identity.
- [ ] **AC8:** PRD/ADR and OpenAPI contracts are updated; generated Go/TS is committed before `make check`; contract and stack smoke tests pass; browser evidence records the back-office form submission and storefront refusal/recovery.

## 2. The architectural decision

Choose **shape d: project immutable adjacency while handling the existing `performance.published` event**.

For a rule-enabled seated map, catalog emits `performance.published` **schema 5**, carrying the exact `seat_map_id` and `orphan_prevention_enabled: true`. Before opening an inventory transaction, the existing `CatalogResolver` fetches `GET /public/seat-maps/{id}` for that exact immutable version and converts its position-ordered rows into left/right adjacency. `ProvisionSeated` then commits the pool, enabled flag, adjacency projection, and consumed event atomically.

Rule-off maps continue emitting today’s byte-pinned schema 4. They make no geometry call and store no adjacency.

At claim time, `CreateSeatHold`:

1. locks the pool;
2. handles idempotency;
3. sweeps expired holds;
4. applies capacity;
5. calls existing `contendedSeats`;
6. only when enabled, reads pool-scoped adjacency plus live `claim_seats`;
7. returns a typed refusal or writes the claim.

This satisfies AC7 because every claimant for the pool serializes on the same row lock, and the orphan decision observes occupancy after the previous claimant commits. The occupancy predicate is `released_at IS NULL` after `sweepExpired`, matching ADR-031 and the unique index.

It satisfies AC4 because an off pool takes the existing schema-4 provisioning route and skips the adjacency query entirely. The existing schema-4 golden and a test that removes the projection table before an off claim pin the absence of hidden reads.

Rejected:

- **a — catalog call inside the claim transaction:** violates ADR-010’s short-transaction boundary and imports network latency/failure while holding the platform’s hottest lock.
- **b — new `seat_map.published` subscription:** needs a new durable, replay/reconciliation, ordering coordination with performance publication, and a stale/missing projection state. The exact immutable map can instead be fetched once during existing provisioning.
- **c — commerce pre-check:** advisory only; parallel claims can both pass, so AC7 is impossible.

This warrants **ADR-041**. It should decide the schema-4/5 fork, provisioning-time exact-version fetch, pool-scoped adjacency projection, lock-local arbitration order, fail-closed behavior, rollout order, and AC4’s “no additional I/O when off” interpretation.

## 3. The test seam

The first failing test goes in `services/inventory/internal/store/seat_claims_smoke_test.go` as `TestSeatHoldRejectsNewlyOrphanedSeats`.

That is the correct TDD seam because it uses real PostgreSQL and directly exercises the deciding transaction, pool lock, lazy expiry, partial index, projection query, typed error, and rollback. Starting at commerce, HTTP, or React could prove error propagation while leaving the concurrency rule advisory.

AC7 also lives here, by extending the existing seated contention proof with the deterministic race:

- row `1–5`;
- claimant A requests seat `1`;
- claimant B requests seat `3`;
- either request is legal alone;
- together they isolate seat `2`;
- exactly one commits and the other returns `orphaned_seats: [2]`.

`smoke/inventory_contention_test.go` remains the GA stack contention suite. Cross-service propagation gets separate coverage in `smoke/checkout_test.go`; it is not the correctness proof.

Run `make generate`, commit all five changed generated files, then run `make check`.

## 5. Design decisions

- **Setting:** `orphan_prevention_enabled boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false` on each `seat_maps` row. `SeatMap` responses always include it. Create defaults off; an edit omitting it inherits the predecessor, while an explicit value applies only to the newly minted version.
- **Projection:** `seat_claim_adjacency` is inventory-owned and pool-scoped. Each seat stores its immediate left/right identity; null explicitly represents a row end. Pool scoping trades duplicated immutable geometry for atomic completeness and eliminates cross-performance projection ambiguity.
- **Transport:** off maps use existing schema 4. Enabled maps use schema 5 with the rule flag and exact map ID; geometry is fetched before the inventory transaction from the existing public exact-version endpoint.
- **Neighbour:** immediate predecessor/successor in the row’s `position` order. Numeric gaps do not create physical gaps; sections and rows never connect.
- **Causality:** reject only seats newly orphaned by this selection. A pre-existing orphan elsewhere does not poison unrelated claims.
- **Row ends:** an end seat has one neighbour. If that neighbour becomes occupied and the end seat remains free, the end seat is orphaned. Selecting the end seat while leaving a run of two or more is allowed. A one-seat row has zero neighbours; selecting it is allowed, and a selection in another row does not newly orphan it.
- **Liveness:** run after `sweepExpired`; occupancy is `claim_seats.released_at IS NULL`, covering held/finalizing/confirmed without counting lazily-unswept expiry.
- **Refusal:** inventory and commerce return HTTP 409 with `code: "orphaned_seats"` and sorted `seat_identities` containing the free seats that would be stranded. A separate typed store error preserves `errors.Is`.
- **Commerce validation:** require a non-empty, unique list disjoint from the requested selection. Do not apply the existing “subset of request” rule; stranded seats are normally not requested. A malformed response is 502.
- **Picker:** reuse `seat-conflict:${slotId}` with typed detail. `seat_taken` keeps today’s unavailable overlay and no-store refresh; `orphaned_seats` shows/highlights the free seats without disabling them or refreshing occupancy. Any selection adjustment clears the warning.
- **Unavailable geometry:** schema-5 resolution failure is delayed-NACKed and no pool is provisioned. The picker consequently fails closed on occupancy. A missing/corrupt adjacency projection discovered at claim time returns inventory 503, commerce 502, and writes nothing.

## 6. Test plan

- Catalog migration proves all pre-existing rows read `false`; enabled rows block a destructive down.
- Catalog store/API tests cover create false/true, required response field, edit inheritance, explicit toggle, and immutable predecessor.
- Exact-version test creates v1 off and v2 on, seats a performance against v1, and proves publication still selects schema 4.
- Event goldens preserve schema-4 bytes for off and pin schema-5 enabled bytes.
- Inventory and access use hand-written schema-5 fixtures; future variants move to schema 6 and remain parked before decoding.
- Resolver tests reject wrong map ID, draft status, disabled-map/schema mismatch, duplicate identities, malformed rows, and non-200 responses.
- Provisioning tests prove pool, flag, adjacency, and `consumed_events` commit together and replay idempotently.
- Core row tests:
  - `1–3`, select `2` → reject `1,3`;
  - `1–3`, select `1` → allow;
  - `1–3`, select `1,2` → reject end seat `3`;
  - two rows with matching positions never become neighbours;
  - position order `10,20,40` still forms two adjacency edges;
  - one-seat row behavior as declared above;
  - return the complete sorted stranded set.
- Lazy-expiry test backdates a hold that would otherwise appear to create an orphan; the claim sweeps it and succeeds.
- Rule-off test repeats an orphan-producing selection and succeeds with the existing response. Dropping `seat_claim_adjacency` before the call proves the disabled branch never reads it.
- Scope test seeds identical identities in another pool and proves no leakage.
- Index proof EXPLAINs the exact shared `orphanedSeatsQuery` under a generic plan after seeding scale; require `seat_claim_adjacency_pkey` and `claim_seats_one_live_per_seat`.
- AC7 contention test races seat `1` against seat `3` in row `1–5`; assert one success, one `OrphanedSeatsError([2])`, and no stranded committed state.
- Inventory handler validates the 409 body; geometry loss validates 503 and rollback.
- Commerce validates forwarding, disjoint identities, and 502 on missing/invalid lists.
- Storefront tests prove the warning is announced, free seats remain enabled, existing selection remains, and a click clears the warning without a reload or occupancy fetch.
- Smoke keeps the existing default-off seated checkout green, then exercises an enabled map: hold seat `3`, reject seat `1` naming `2`, and accept adjusted selection `1,2`.
- Browser evidence under `make up`:
  - submit the real back-office create/edit form with the setting enabled;
  - select `1,3` on a five-seat row in the storefront;
  - observe the 409 warning naming seat `2`;
  - add `2` or deselect a neighbour and reserve successfully without reloading.

## 7. Risks

1. **Hot transaction regression:** the enabled query runs under the pool lock. Bound it to at most two candidates per requested seat, use the two named indexes, EXPLAIN the production query, and retain the rule-off no-read trap.
2. **Schema rollout skew:** catalog emitting schema 5 before inventory/access understand it makes both consumers park and readiness fall. Deploy migrations and consumers first; hand-written schema-5/6 tests and smoke readiness catch drift.
3. **Expired holds counted as occupied:** raw `released_at IS NULL` before sweeping would reject legal choices. The explicit backdated-hold test catches ordering regressions.
4. **Wrong map version:** resolving the family’s current version would silently change a live pool’s rule. The v1/v2 performance-publication test and stored exact map ID catch it.
5. **Partial or malformed projection:** a missing neighbour could allow an orphan. Provision atomically, validate every row before storing, and fail closed on missing requested adjacency.
6. **Free stranded seats rendered as taken:** reusing the current array-only event blindly would disable the repair path. Typed event detail, DOM tests, and browser evidence catch this.
7. **Commerce semantic validation copied from `seat_taken`:** requiring the identities to be a request subset would convert every valid orphan refusal to 502. Dedicated forwarding tests pin disjoint semantics.
8. **Back-office form wiring:** component/render tests cannot catch Astro origin or form-data behavior. Real browser submission is mandatory per the repository learning.

## 8. Open decisions

- **“New orphan” versus “any orphan after selection”:** choose newly caused orphans. Existing isolated seats—possibly from refunds or administrative history—must not block unrelated rows forever.
- **Adjacency representation:** choose immediate neighbours derived from row `position`, not label arithmetic or visual coordinates. It is deterministic and survives non-numeric labels and position gaps.
- **Projection scope:** choose per inventory pool, not globally per map. It duplicates immutable data but makes provisioning completeness, version binding, and claim scoping local and atomic.
- **Event shape:** choose schema 5 only for enabled seated maps. Off maps retain the existing schema-4 golden and avoid the provisioning geometry fetch.
- **Failure posture:** choose fail closed: delayed NAK before provisioning, 503/502 if projection integrity is later missing.
- **Wire code:** choose `orphaned_seats`, distinct from `seat_taken`; the identities describe free stranded seats, not seats lost to another buyer.
- **AC4 wording:** interpret “no extra latency” as no additional network call, SQL statement, lock, or projection access on the disabled claim path. Literal zero timing difference is not measurable and is impossible to guarantee after any code change; if nanosecond equality is intended, AC4 is impossible as written.

<!-- sdlc:stage=plan-review kind=plan -->
### Adversarial plan critique — TKT-175

**Critiqued by `main-agent` (Claude Opus 5)**, per `config.models.planReview`. Cross-model check holds.

**Verdict: ACCEPT the architecture. REJECT the sizing.** The ticket as scoped is not one ticket, and the plan is what proves it.

---

#### The architecture is right, and it found an option the decomposition did not have

The decomposition offered three shapes and the draft rejected all three, correctly:

| | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| a — catalog call inside the claim transaction | a network round trip while holding the platform's hottest lock; ADR-010 exists to prevent exactly this |
| b — new `seat_map.published` subscription | a new durable, replay and reconciliation, ordering against performance publication, and a projection that can be stale or missing |
| c — commerce pre-check | **advisory**, so parallel claimants can both pass. AC7 is not merely hard, it is impossible |

Its own answer — **shape d** — is better than all three and turns on one observation I had not made: **a published seat-map version is immutable (ADR-029)**. So the geometry can be fetched *once, at provisioning time*, for that exact version, and projected into inventory. There is no staleness to reconcile because the thing projected cannot change. That removes (b)'s entire cost while keeping (a)'s accuracy and (c)'s hot-path silence, and the claim-time check then runs under the pool lock that TKT-173 already made the arbitration point (`contendedSeats`).

Two further judgements worth keeping:

- **"Newly orphaned", not "any orphan after selection."** A seat stranded earlier — by a refund, by an admin action — must not poison unrelated claims for ever. This is the difference between a rule and a trap.
- **AC4 read honestly.** "No extra latency" is interpreted as *no additional network call, SQL statement, lock, or projection access* on the disabled path, and the draft says plainly that literal timing equality is unmeasurable and, if intended, makes the AC impossible. It also proposes the right test: **drop the projection table and prove a rule-off claim still succeeds.** That is an absence proven by construction rather than asserted.

The `orphaned_seats` code being distinct from `seat_taken` is also right, and the reason is subtle: these identities are **free seats the buyer did not ask for**, so commerce's TKT-173 "must be a subset of the request" validation would reject every valid refusal as malformed. The draft caught that; it is exactly the kind of cross-ticket interaction that ships broken.

#### Finding — SIZING: this is four tickets wearing one ticket's name

The plan's own file list is the evidence: **~50 files across five services**, plus two UIs, plus an ADR, plus a new PRD section. Specifically it contains:

1. a catalog setting (migration, store, contract, back-office form, browser evidence);
2. a **domain-event schema fork** — `performance.published` schema 5 — with ADR-017 obligations and a **cross-service rollout ordering** (catalog must not emit 5 until inventory *and* access accept it, or both consumers park and readiness falls);
3. an inventory geometry projection (migration, new table, resolver, provisioning atomicity);
4. the claim-time rule itself plus its contention proof;
5. a storefront refusal surface with semantics deliberately different from the existing one.

Any one of 1, 2+3, 4, or 5 is a reviewable slice. Together they are ~2000 lines and a Gate-3 diff no human reads in one sitting — the exact thing `decomposition.md`'s sizing rule exists to prevent (*"one ticket = one vertical slice a human can review in one sitting… target ~≤ 400 changed lines"*).

**This is a defect in my decomposition, not in the plan.** At decomposition I recorded the architectural question as an open uncertainty and sized the ticket as though answering it were the only cost. The answer turned out to carry a schema fork and a projection with it. The draft could not have made this smaller without making it wrong — and it did not pretend otherwise, which is the correct behaviour.

#### The rollout constraint that makes the split mandatory rather than tidy

Risk 2 in the plan is the sharpest thing in it: *"catalog emitting schema 5 before inventory/access understand it makes both consumers park and readiness fall."* ADR-017 §5b′ requires a consumer to dispatch on `schema` **before** decoding `data`. So the safe order is **consumers first, producer second** — and that ordering is only expressible as separate merges. Shipping producer and consumers in one PR does not violate the ADR, but it forfeits the ability to deploy them in the order the ADR's own reasoning demands.

#### Verdict

**Split.** The architecture, the ADR, and every design decision above carry over unchanged into the children — the thinking is done and it is good. Only the delivery is re-cut.
